extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent claim is "directed to" an abstract idea under the Alice/Mayo framework (MPEP Step 2A), including categories courts have identified as abstract and examples of claims that are or are not directed to abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on case-identified concepts, not judicial descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should rely on the substantive concepts identified in court decisions (the underlying concepts), not merely the shorthand judicial descriptors/labels when determining whether a claimed concept is similar to a court-identified abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mechanically match a claim to a judicial label (e.g., 'fundamental economic practice'); instead analyze whether the claim recites a concept similar to the concepts courts found abstract. Use the cases cited as conceptual guides rather than fixed labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim is directed to an abstract idea only if the claim recites the abstract idea (MPEP Step 2A requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Step 2A, a claim must recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea in order to be 'directed to' that abstract idea. Not all inventions that embody or use abstract ideas are necessarily 'directed to' them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind Alice/Mayo: while all inventions may use laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas at some level, Step 2A separates claims that explicitly recite abstract ideas from those that merely may be based on them. Evaluate the claim language for whether it sets forth or describes an abstract concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a claim is based on or involves an abstract idea but does not recite it, it is not directed to the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are based on or involve an abstract idea but do not actually recite anything similar to a judicially-identified abstract idea are not 'directed to' an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and relevant cases: Enfish (self-referential table — based on but not directed to organizing information), DDR Holdings (modifying hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpages — not directed to previously identified abstract ideas), Trading Technologies (graphical UI improving trader accuracy — not directed). Non-limiting hypotheticals include purely structural or physical device claims (printer, washing machine, earring with sensor), a BRCA1 sequencing method, BIOS loading into volatile memory — these may be based on abstract concepts in the broadest sense but do not recite judicially-identified abstract ideas and thus are not 'directed to' them.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a claim recites an abstract idea but the claim as a whole is directed to an improvement (or otherwise does not seek to tie up the abstract idea), it is not directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite an abstract idea can nevertheless not be 'directed to' that idea when, as a whole, they recite additional elements (such as a technological improvement) showing the claim does not tie up the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the additional elements represent a specific improvement to computer-related technology or other concrete technological improvement (see MPEP §§2106.05(a) and 2106.06(b)). Cases: McRO (automated lip-synchronization and facial animation — improvement in computer-related technology), Enfish (self-referential table — specific improvement in computer operation), Research Corp. (blue-noise mask plus additional steps improving computer functioning). Non-limiting hypotheticals: surgical shears with pressure regulator, robotic arm assembly with sensor/control for smooth motion, autofocus camera system with processor/algorithm/drive mechanism, internal combustion engine with EGR control system — these examples illustrate improvements that render eligibility self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of concepts courts have identified as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have repeatedly identified several broad categories of concepts that are commonly treated as abstract ideas: (I) fundamental economic practices; (II) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (III) an idea 'of itself' (mental processes, concepts performable in the human mind or by pen-and-paper, or ideas with no particular concrete form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Use these categories as signposts when comparing claim concepts to judicially-identified abstractions. The MPEP enumerates subtypes and many cases as examples:
- I. Fundamental economic practices: concepts relating to economy/commerce such as agreements/contracts, performance of financial transactions (buySAFE), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs.), hedging (Bilski), processing financing applications, rules for wagering games (In re Smith), etc. Also includes mitigating financial risk/intermediated settlement (Alice).
- II. Certain methods of organizing human activity: concepts relating to managing relationships/transactions or legal obligations (buySAFE, Dealertrack, Bancorp), advertising/marketing/sales activities (Ameranth, Ultramercial), managing human behavior (budgeting/tracking spending — Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One), and tracking/organizing information (BASCOM, TLI Communications, Electric Power Group).
- III. An idea 'of itself': mental processes and information manipulation that can be performed mentally or with pen-and-paper (CyberSource, Ambry Genetics, Synopsys), collecting/analyzing/displaying information (Content Extraction, FairWarning, Electric Power Group), data comparisons analogous to human mental work (CyberSource, Mortgage Grader), and concepts described as having no particular concrete or tangible form (Ultramercial — using advertising as exchange).
Examples in guidance: collecting, comparing, classifying, encoding/decoding, organizing via mathematical correlations, creating indices, relaying mailing address data, retaining navigation info in online forms. Courts have treated mere presentation of results of abstract processes without more as abstract (Content Extraction, Ultramercial, Content Extraction & Transmission).
